lead: Honolulu's water damage is mostly vertical. In a city of high-rise condos, one burst pipe or overflowing tub can soak several units below before anyone finds it.
risk: condo leaks, aging building plumbing and heavy rain
risk_short: condo leaks, old building pipes, heavy rain
why: Honolulu has more high-rise homes than almost any U.S. city, and many towers in Waikiki, Makiki and Kakaako went up in the 1960s and 1970s. Their original pipes are now wearing out. A failed supply line, water heater or drain stack can send water down through floors and walls into the units below. Salt air also speeds up corrosion on pipes and fittings.

Condo leaks raise hard questions about who pays. The building's master policy usually covers common pipes and walls, while each owner covers their own unit and belongings. Heavy rain is the other risk. Winter storms called Kona lows can dump inches of rain in a few hours, and water pours down the valleys into Manoa, Kalihi and other low areas. In this warm, humid climate, mold grows fast.
image_alt: Worker painting a ceiling with a long roller
image_caption: After a leak from the unit above, a Honolulu condo ceiling is dried, patched and repainted.
problems: Valley homes in Manoa, Kalihi, Nuuanu
tips: Know where your unit's water shutoff valve is.
Replace washer and toilet supply hoses every five years.
Read your association's master policy and your HO-6 coverage.
Add a leak sensor under sinks and the water heater.
areas: Calls come from Waikiki, Kaimuki, Manoa, Kakaako, Kalihi, Makiki, Moiliili and Nuuanu, plus Aiea, Pearl City and Kailua.

faq.q: Who pays when a leak from the condo above damages my Honolulu unit?
faq.a: It depends on the source and your building's rules. If a pipe in a common wall failed, the association's master policy usually responds. If the upstairs owner's tub or appliance overflowed, their HO-6 policy may pay. Your own HO-6 covers your belongings and fixtures. Document everything with photos.
